User Research & Usability Testing Basics ## A Real‑World Wake‑Up Call Imagine you’ve just spent a week polishing a high‑fidelity onboarding flow in **Figma** for a fintech startup. The screens look sleek, the micro‑interactions are snappy, and the design system you built in the previous module is humming. The product manager is thrilled—until the first user clicks “Next” and the app crashes on the third screen. Suddenly the polished UI feels useless because the underlying flow isn’t intuitive. That moment is where **User Research & Usability Testing** become the safety net that turns a beautiful prototype into a *usable* product. In this chapter you’ll learn how to plan low‑cost tests, extract actionable insights, and iterate directly in Figma so that each design decision is backed by real user behavior. --- ## 1. Picking the Right Low‑Cost Research Method When budgets are tight and timelines are tight, you don’t need a full‑scale lab study. The goal is to surface the biggest usability problems quickly. Below are the most practical methods for an intermediate designer who already has a high‑fidelity prototype. | Method | When to Use It | Core Benefits | Typical Cost | |--------|----------------|---------------|--------------| | **Guerrilla Testing** | Public spaces, coffee shops, coworking areas | Immediate feedback, diverse participants | $0–$50 (snacks, incentives) | | **Remote Unmoderated Test** (e.g., Lookback, Maze) | Distributed audience, asynchronous schedule | Scalable, cheap, data automatically recorded | Free tier → $20–$100 per month | | **Remote Moderated Test** (Zoom + Figma share) | Complex tasks that need clarification | Real‑time probing, high‑quality qualitative data | Free‑tier video conferencing | | **Think‑Aloud Protocol** | Any setting where you can observe the user | Reveals mental model, uncovers hidden assumptions | No extra cost beyond participant incentive | | **Post‑Task Survey / SUS** | After any test | Quantifies perceived usability, easy to compare over time | Free (Google Forms, Typeform) | > **Tip:** Start with a single method—often guerrilla testing or a remote unmoderated test—and expand only if you need deeper insight. --- ## 2. Planning a Usability Test A well‑structured test saves time, respects participants, and yields clean data. Follow this checklist before you hit “record.” 1. **Define Clear Goals** *What do you want to learn?* - Example: “Validate that new users can complete the onboarding flow in under 2 minutes without assistance.” 2. **Select Representative Participants** - Target the **primary persona** you created in the Empathy Map (e.g., “Busy Millennials who manage multiple financial accounts”). - Aim for **5‑7 participants**; research shows this sample size uncovers ~85 % of major usability issues. 3. **Create a Test Script** - **Intro**: Brief context, consent, and a reminder to think aloud. - **Tasks**: Written as *goal‑oriented* statements, e.g., “Sign up for a new account and set a spending limit.” - **Closing**: Open‑ended questions about overall impressions. 4. **Define Success Criteria & Metrics** - **Quantitative**: Task Completion Rate, Time on Task, Error Rate, SUS score. - **Qualitative**: Observed confusion, verbalized frustration, “I don’t know what to do next.” 5. **Choose a Recording Tool** - For **remote unmoderated** tests, platforms like **Maze** capture screen video and click data automatically. - For **moderated** sessions, use **Zoom** with *record* enabled and share the Figma prototype via a public link. 6. **Prepare Incentives** - A modest gift card ($10‑$15) or a free month of the app is enough to motivate participants without blowing the budget. ### Quick Planning Template (Copy‑Paste) ``` Goal: ________________________________________________ Participants: ________________________________________ Tasks: 1. ________________________________________________ 2. ________________________________________________ 3. ________________________________________________ Metrics: - Completion Rate: ______% - Avg. Time: _______ seconds - SUS: _______/100 ``` --- ## 3. Running the Test: From Figma to the Participant ### 3.1. Setting Up the Prototype for Testing 1. **Publish a Shareable Link** - In Figma, click **Share → Copy Link** and set the permissions to **Anyone with the link can view**. 2. **Enable Presentation Mode** - Click the **Play** button to open the prototype in a new tab; this removes the UI chrome and mimics a real app. 3. **Add Interaction Hints (Optional)** - If you anticipate a tricky step, embed a temporary tooltip component that you’ll later remove. This keeps the test focused on the core flow rather than accidental clicks. ### 3.2. Conducting the Session | Step | Moderator Action | Participant Action | |------|------------------|--------------------| | **1. Warm‑up** | Small talk, explain think‑aloud rule. | Relax, begin verbalizing. | | **2. Task Intro** | Read the task verbatim, avoid leading language. | Listen, start the task. | | **3. Observation** | Keep a **silent** posture, note only when the participant pauses or hesitates. | Interact with the prototype. | | **4. Probing** | When stuck > “What are you thinking right now?” | Explain mental process. | | **5. Wrap‑up** | Ask “What would have made this easier?” | Provide open feedback. | **Do NOT**: Offer hints or solutions during the test. The goal is to see where the design fails, not to coach the user. ### 3.3. Capturing Data - **Screen Recording**: Built‑in to most remote tools; ensures you can replay exact clicks. - **Audio**: Capture the think‑aloud commentary. - **Notes**: Use a two‑column table (Observation | Quote) to keep raw data tidy. - **Metrics Logging**: Have a simple spreadsheet ready to tick off task completion, time, and errors on the spot. --- ## 4. Analyzing Results: Turning Chaos into Insight ### 4.1. Organize the Raw Data 1. **Transcribe Key Quotes** - Pull out any verbatim statements that reveal confusion or delight. 2. **Log Quantitative Scores** - Compute averages for Time on Task, Completion Rate, and SUS. ### 4.2. Affinity Mapping (The “Cluster” Method) - **Step 1:** Write each observation (both quantitative and qualitative) on a sticky note (physical or digital – Miro works well). - **Step 2:** Group notes by similarity: *Navigation Issues*, *Terminology Confusion*, *Visual Clarity*, *Feedback Gaps*. - **Step 3:** Label each cluster and note the **frequency** (how many participants mentioned it). ### 4.3. Severity Rating Use a simple 1‑3 scale to prioritize fixes: | Severity | Description | |----------|-------------| | **1 – Minor** | Cosmetic or isolated issue; affects < 20 % of users. | | **2 – Moderate** | Causes hesitation or a single error; affects 20‑60 % of users. | | **3 – Critical** | Blocks task completion or leads to repeated errors; affects > 60 % of users. | Place each cluster into the appropriate severity bucket. The highest‑severity items become your immediate design targets. ### 4.4. Crafting Insight Statements Structure each insight as: > **[User type]** *struggles with* **[specific problem]** *because* **[reason]**, *leading to* **[negative outcome]**. **Example:** > **Busy Millennials** struggle with **finding the “Set Spending Limit” toggle** because the toggle is hidden inside a collapsible “Advanced Settings” section, leading to **abandonment of the onboarding flow**. These statements bridge the gap between raw data and actionable design decisions. --- ## 5. Iterating in Figma: From Insight to Solution ### 5.1. Prioritizing Fixes Apply the **MoSCoW** method (Must, Should, Could, Won’t) to the severity‑rated list: - **Must**: Critical (Severity 3) – must be addressed before the next release. - **Should**: Moderate (Severity 2) – schedule for the upcoming sprint. - **Could**: Minor (Severity 1) – backlog for future polish. ### 5.2. Making Rapid Changes with Components Because you already built a **design system**, updating the flow is straightforward: 1. **Locate the Affected Component** - Use **Figma’s “Search” (⌘ / F)** to find the component name (e.g., `Toggle – Advanced`). 2. **Create a Variant** - Add a new variant called `Visible` that shows the toggle on the main screen. 3. **Swap Instances** - Select all instances on the onboarding screens and switch to the new variant with a single click. *Result:* The visual change propagates automatically, preserving consistency across the prototype. ### 5.3. Updating Interaction Flows If a task required an extra step that caused confusion, rewrite the flow: - **Original:** `Screen A → (Tap) → Screen B (Collapsible) → Screen C` - **Revised:** `Screen A → (Tap) → Screen C` (remove the collapsible step). Use **Auto‑Layout** to realign elements after removing a section, ensuring spacing stays uniform. ### 5.4. Documenting the Iteration Add a **Version History** page in your Figma file: | Version | Date | Change Summary | Reason (Insight) | |---------|------|----------------|------------------| | v1.2 | 07‑26‑2026 | Exposed “Spending Limit” toggle on Screen 2 | Critical usability issue (users couldn’t locate toggle) | | v1.3 | 07‑30‑2026 | Added inline validation for email field | Moderate issue (error messages unclear) | This documentation becomes part of the **Deliverables** you’ll hand off to developers later, linking each design decision to a concrete user problem. --- ## 6. Closing the Loop: From Test to Next Test Usability testing is not a one‑off event. The **Iterative Framework** you’ve been using (Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test → Implement) cycles continuously. After you’ve updated the prototype: 1. **Run a Quick Follow‑Up Test** - Use the same participants (if possible) or a fresh set to verify that the critical issue is resolved. 2. **Compare Metrics** - Look for improvements in Completion Rate, Time on Task, and SUS. A 15‑20 % lift is a good early indicator. 3. **Decide Next Steps** - If the issue persists, revisit the insight statement and consider alternative solutions (e.g., redesigning the entire onboarding flow). The **feedback loop** becomes tighter each time you repeat this process, turning your design into a living artifact that evolves with real user needs. --- ## 7. Communicating Findings & Design Decisions Even though this chapter focuses on the hands‑on side, the **deliverables** you produce matter for stakeholder alignment: - **Usability Test Report** (2–3 pages) - Goals, Method, Participants, Key Findings (clustered), Severity Ratings, Suggested Fixes. - **Annotated Figma Prototype** - Use Figma’s **Comment** feature to attach insights directly onto affected frames. - **Design Update Log** (the version history table above). When you present these artifacts, tie each design change back to a specific user quote. This narrative makes the rationale crystal clear and builds trust with product managers and developers. --- ## Key Takeaways - **Low‑cost methods**—guerrilla testing, remote unmoderated tests, and think‑aloud protocols—are sufficient to uncover the most severe usability problems. - **Plan rigorously:** define goals, recruit the right participants, script tasks, and decide on success metrics before you start testing. - **Capture both quantitative** (completion rate, time, SUS) **and qualitative** data (verbalized confusion) to get a full picture of the user experience. - **Analyze with affinity mapping and severity rating** to prioritize what to fix first. - **Iterate directly in Figma** using components, variants, and auto‑layout; document every change in a version‑history page. - **Close the loop** by running a follow‑up test, measuring metric improvements, and feeding new insights back into the next design cycle. By embedding these research habits into your workflow, you’ll turn every high‑fidelity prototype from a static showcase into a **validated, user‑centric solution** ready for development. --- # Chapter 8: 8. Accessibility & Inclusive Design Principles ## A Real‑World Prompt: Designing a Dashboard for All Users Imagine you’re tasked with redesigning the home screen of a health‑tracking app that will be used by a diverse audience—busy professionals, seniors with declining vision, and users who rely on screen readers. The brief calls for a clean, data‑rich layout that feels modern, yet every user must be able to read the numbers, navigate with a keyboard, and understand the content through a screen reader. How do you turn this vision into a concrete, inclusive UI in Figma? The answer lies in weaving **accessibility** into every design decision, not tacking it on at the end. This chapter shows you how to embed WCAG contrast ratios, text‑size guidelines, keyboard‑first navigation, and screen‑reader friendliness directly into your Figma workflow, then validate those decisions with the right plugins and checklists. --- ## 1. Quick Primer on WCAG and Why It Matters The **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)** are the industry‑standard reference for making digital products perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. For UI designers, the most immediately actionable WCAG success criteria are: | Principle | WCAG Success Criterion | What It Means for UI | |-----------|------------------------|----------------------| | **Perceivable** | **1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)** – Text and images of text must have a contrast ratio of **≥ 4.5:1** (AA) or **≥ 7:1** (AAA) | Choose foreground/background color pairs that meet the ratio. | | **Perceivable** | **1.4.4 Resize Text** – Text must be resizable up to **200 %** without loss of content or functionality | Use relative units (rem, em) and avoid fixed‑size containers that clip enlarged text. | | **Operable** | **2.1.1 Keyboard** – All functionality must be operable through a keyboard interface | Ensure focus order, visible focus indicators, and avoid keyboard traps. | | **Understandable** | **2.4.6 Headings and Labels** – Proper semantic headings aid screen‑reader navigation | Use clear hierarchy in component naming and layer organization. | These criteria map directly onto the objectives of this module. Throughout the chapter you’ll see concrete ways to satisfy them in Figma, turning abstract numbers into visual decisions you can see and test instantly. --- ## 2. Applying Contrast Ratios in Figma ### 2.1. Set Up a Contrast Palette 1. **Create a “Color Tokens” page** in your design system file (see Chapter 5 on Design Systems). 2. Add a **Contrast Matrix** component that lists primary, secondary, and neutral colors alongside their WCAG ratios when paired with background options (e.g., white, dark‑gray). 3. Use the **Figma “Color Contrast Checker” plugin** to automatically calculate ratios for any pair you input. > **Tip:** Keep the matrix visible while you design. When you drag a new color onto a button or text layer, the plugin updates the ratio in real time, nudging you toward compliant choices before the design is even finished. ### 2.2. Practical Contrast Workflows | Situation | Recommended Ratio | How to Achieve It in Figma | |-----------|-------------------|----------------------------| | Body copy on a light background | **≥ 4.5:1** (AA) | Use dark gray (`#212121`) on white (`#FFFFFF`). Verify with the plugin; if you prefer a softer tone, raise the opacity of the text color until the ratio passes. | | Large headings (≥ 24 pt) on a colored card | **≥ 3:1** (AA for large text) | Choose a slightly lighter foreground (e.g., `#FFFFFF` on `#0066CC`). Since large text gets a relaxed ratio, you have more flexibility, but still check the exact value. | | Interactive icons on a dark toolbar | **≥ 3:1** (AA for non‑text) | Apply a bright accent color (`#FFCC00`) against the toolbar’s dark background (`#2B2B2B`). Use the plugin to confirm the ratio. | ### 2.3. Dealing with Images of Text If your design includes **images that contain text** (e.g., a promotional banner), WCAG 1.4.5 requires an alternative text or a **text‑only version**. In Figma: 1. **Layer the text** as a separate component on top of the image. 2. Add a **“Text Alternative”** field to the component’s description (right‑click → “Edit description”). 3. When exporting, the development handoff will include the alt text automatically. --- ## 3. Text Size, Typography, and Responsive Scaling ### 3.1. Base Font Size and Relative Units - **Set a base font size of 16 px** (or 1 rem) on the root frame. - Define all typographic styles using **rem values** in the design system (e.g., `1.125 rem` for body, `1.5 rem` for headings). - When you need a larger display heading, use `2 rem` or higher. This ensures that when a user zooms the page to 200 %, the hierarchy remains proportional. ### 3.2. Figma Tricks for Text Resizability 1. **Enable “Auto Layout”** for containers that hold text. This lets the container grow automatically as the text size increases. 2. **Avoid fixed‑height frames** for text blocks; use “hug contents” so that enlarged text doesn’t get clipped. 3. **Test scaling**: Select the root frame, then use **Zoom → 200 %** (or the plugin “Responsive Resize”). Verify that no content overflows or becomes hidden. ### 3.3. Line Height and Letter Spacing for Legibility - **Line height** should be at least **1.5×** the font size for body copy. - **Letter spacing** (tracking) can be slightly increased for uppercase headings to improve readability. - In Figma, create **Text Style tokens** that embed these ratios, making it impossible to accidentally apply a cramped line height. --- ## 4. Designing for Keyboard Navigation Keyboard accessibility is often overlooked in visual design, yet it’s a core WCAG requirement. The goal is to make every interactive element reachable, identifiable, and operable with **Tab**, **Enter**, **Space**, and **Arrow** keys. ### 4.1. Establish a Logical Tab Order 1. **Group interactive elements** into logical sections (e.g., navigation → main content → footer). 2. In Figma, use **Layers → Order** to arrange components in the same order you want the tab sequence. The plugin **“Tab Order Inspector”** reads this order and flags mismatches. 3. For modal dialogs, ensure the focus is **trapped** inside the modal (i.e., tabbing cycles within the dialog). Add a **“Focus Trap”** annotation to the component. ### 4.2. Visible Focus Indicators A visible focus ring tells sighted keyboard users where they are. - **Design a focus style** in your component library (e.g., a 2 px outline in the brand accent color). - Apply this style to **all interactive components** using a **Component Variant** named “Focused”. - In the prototype, simulate focus by adding a **“Keyboard” interaction** that switches to the “Focused” variant when the element receives a `focus` event. ### 4.3. Avoid Keyboard Traps A keyboard trap occurs when a user cannot exit a component using the Tab key. To prevent this in Figma: 1. **Link the last focusable element** of a modal to the first element using a **“Keyboard” interaction** (`Shift+Tab`). 2. Use the **“A11y Checker” plugin** to scan for elements that lack a forward or backward focus path. --- ## 5. Making Screens Readable by Screen Readers Screen readers translate UI elements into spoken words. For them to work well, the UI must be **semantic** and **well‑labeled**. ### 5.1. Semantic Naming Conventions - **Name layers** with their purpose, not just visual description (e.g., “Primary Button – Submit” instead of “Blue Rounded Rect”). - **Group components** under meaningful frames (e.g., `Header`, `Main Content`, `Footer`). - The plugin **“Accessibility Linter”** checks for ambiguous names and suggests improvements. ### 5.2. ARIA‑like Labels in Figma While Figma doesn’t generate real ARIA attributes, you can **embed them in component descriptions**: 1. Select a component → “Edit description”. 2. Add a line like: `aria-label: “Search field, enter query and press Enter”`. 3. When developers hand off the design, they can copy these lines into the codebase. ### 5.3. Hidden but Accessible Text Sometimes you need **off‑screen instructions** (e.g., “Press Esc to close this dialog”). In Figma: - Create a **text layer** with the instruction. - Set its **opacity to 0%** and **disable “Clip content”** so it doesn’t affect layout. - Add a description tag `sr-only` so developers know to apply the appropriate CSS class. --- ## 6. Collaborative Validation - **Invite developers** to view the prototype in **Figma’s “Presentation” mode**. They can test keyboard navigation directly in the browser. - **Record a short walkthrough** (using Figma’s built‑in video export) that highlights focus states and contrast compliance. Share the video with QA teams for an extra layer of verification. --- ## 7. Embedding Inclusive Design Mindset in Your Workflow Accessibility isn’t a checklist; it’s a **design philosophy** that starts at the ideation stage. ### 7.1. Empathy Mapping for Diverse Users Recall the **Empathy Map** from Chapter 7. Add a “Accessibility” quadrant that captures: - **Say:** “I need big text.” - **Think:** “Will I be able to navigate without a mouse?” - **Feel:** “Frustrated when I can’t see contrast.” - **Do:** “Use a screen reader.” When you sketch user stories, include **accessibility acceptance criteria** (e.g., “As a user with low vision, I can read all copy at 200 % zoom without horizontal scrolling”). ### 7.2. Prototyping with Accessibility in Mind When building **high‑fidelity prototypes** (see Chapter 5), enable **Keyboard Interactions** and **VoiceOver simulation**: 1. In Prototype settings, turn on “Keyboard navigation”. 2. Use the **“Screen Reader” toggle** (available in the prototype preview) to hear how a screen reader would read each element. 3. Adjust component labels and focus indicators based on the feedback. --- ## 8. Bringing It All Together: A Step‑by‑Step Walkthrough Below is a concise workflow you can follow for any new screen, using the health‑app dashboard scenario as an example. 1. **Define Requirements** - From the brief, note: “Numbers must be readable at 200 % zoom”, “All buttons reachable via Tab”, “Screen reader announces chart titles”. 2. **Set Up Tokens** - Open the **Design System** file. - Verify that **Color Tokens** include contrast‑approved pairs. - Confirm **Typography Tokens** use rem units and meet line‑height guidelines. 3. **Create the Layout** - Use **Auto Layout** for containers. - Place text components using the predefined **Text Styles**. 4. **Apply Contrast** - Select each text layer → run **Contrast Checker** → adjust color until the ratio meets AA. - For chart legends, ensure the color markers also meet the required contrast against the chart background. 5. **Add Focus Styles** - Duplicate each interactive component variant → rename to “Focused”. - Apply a 2 px accent outline. 6. **Define Keyboard Flow** - Order layers to match visual reading order. - Run **Tab Order Inspector** → fix any out‑of‑order arrows. 7. **Add Screen‑Reader Labels** - Edit component descriptions with `aria-label` text. - Insert hidden “sr‑only” instructions where needed. 8. **Run the Validation Suite** - Execute **A11y Checker** → resolve any flagged issues. - Perform a **Responsive Resize** at 200 % zoom → confirm no overflow. 9. **Document in Checklist** - Tick each item on the **Accessibility Checklist** page. 10. **Share for Review** - Present the prototype to a teammate using **Presentation mode**. - Record a short video showing focus movement and contrast verification.
